newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Half-apology by the president angers S.Koreans.
newsitem.headline: Half-apology by the president angers S.Koreans.

text.p: South Korean president Kim Young-sam, fighting to rescue his adminstration, apologised for election spending abuses on Friday but defiantly refused to offer any details of his finances.
Instead, Kim challenged opponents who accuse him of overspending in the 1992 presidential polls to help clean up the system. And he suggested they were just as guilty.

His remarks, part contrite and part combatative, were broadcast live on television. Far from defusing a crisis, they appeared only to sharpen the battle lines between the opposition and a president already deeply wounded by a related corruption scandal and the arrest of his son.
A solemn-faced Kim noted that his 1992 campaign spending had been "raised as a problem in political circles".
"For this, first of all, I and our entire political circle must bow our heads to the public and repent of past wrongdoings," he said.
But he added: "I'm sure you understand it is impossible to reveal the entire size of funds and spending from five years ago during a hectic election campaign."

Opposition parties allege that Kim's 1992 election was partly bankrolled by the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group and his disgraced predecessor, Roh Tae-woo. They say the campaign grossly exceeded legal spending limits.
Kim's opponents are treading on difficult ground, since leaders of all political parties are widely assumed to have overspent on elections.
Kim, however, is especially vulnerable since he was swept to power pledging to sever the corrupt collusion between politicians and big business.
"President Kim's speech ended by avoiding and shifting all responsibility," said a spokeswoman for the largest opposition party, the National Congress for New Politics.
"We will use all means to fight to reveal the truth," Park Sun-suck said. "We will try to call President Kim Young-sam to a National Assembly hearing as a witness."

Ordinary South Koreans appeared disappointed at an apology that fell far short of the act of personal contrition that many had expected. Kim is due to step down at the end of his single term next February, but scandals swirling around him have paralysed his administration.
There have been veiled calls for Kim to step down before presidential polls in December.
"The speech didn't say anything important. I felt deeply deceived," said Kim Young-jun, an elderly man watching the live broadcast on a screen at Seoul's main train station.
"President Kim should have revealed how much money was used in the election, said businessman Kim In-suk, his face red with anger. "He can't tell us he doesn't know."
Kim called on all parties to help draft new election financing legislation, and warned that unless they cooperated he would make a "grave resolution". He did not elaborate.
At one point, Kim went on the offensive against his opponents.

"If you really worry about the difficulties this country faces, and if you really regret the faulty political climate, I hope you will stop the national drift with wasteful discussions of the election funds," Kim said.
He was referring to the faltering economy, which has added to a sense of national crisis.

The president's immediate woes stem from the collapse in January of Hanbo Steel Co, which uncovered a web of corruption linking the company to his top aides. State prosecutors allege that politicians took bribes from Hanbo for help in arranging loans worth five trillion won ($5.6 billion).

It was Kim's second apology over the so-called "Hanbogate" scandal, which led to the arrest of his second son, Kim Hyun-chul, this month. He first expressed remorse in a televised speech to the nation in February.
"The results of the 'Hanbo incident' showed all of us the depth of the roots of corruption and the links between business and politics," Kim said.
